title: FHA Foreclosure Timeline and Servicing Compliance — CTL Policy
content:
FHA Foreclosure Timeline and Servicing Compliance Policy — CTL Requirements for FHA-Insured Properties.

Purpose: Properties with FHA-insured mortgages are subject to HUD's servicing timeline requirements. Non-compliance with these timelines can result in curtailment of the insurance claim, meaning the servicer absorbs costs that would otherwise be covered by FHA insurance. This policy establishes the timeline verification requirements for CTL determination on FHA properties.

Section 1 — Default and Loss Mitigation Timeline:
Before initiating foreclosure on an FHA-insured mortgage, the servicer must comply with the loss mitigation requirements of Regulation X (12 CFR Part 1024, Subpart C). Key timeline milestones: (a) Early intervention — servicer must attempt to contact the borrower by the 36th day of delinquency. (b) Written notice — servicer must provide written notice of loss mitigation options no later than the 45th day of delinquency. (c) Loss mitigation evaluation — if the borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application more than 37 days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, the servicer must evaluate the application. (d) Dual tracking prohibition — the servicer may not move forward with foreclosure while a loss mitigation application is pending evaluation, per CFPB Regulation X.

Section 2 — First Legal Action Deadlines:
HUD prescribes maximum deadlines for first legal action (filing of foreclosure complaint or posting of notice of default). These deadlines are measured from the date of default and vary by state based on the foreclosure process type: Non-judicial foreclosure states (e.g., Texas, California, Georgia): Generally within 6 months of default. Judicial foreclosure states (e.g., New York, New Jersey, Florida): Generally within 6 to 9 months of default, reflecting longer judicial timelines. State-specific reasonable diligence timelines are published by HUD and updated periodically.

Section 3 — Foreclosure Completion Deadlines:
HUD also monitors the elapsed time from first legal action to foreclosure completion. Servicers are expected to complete foreclosure within the reasonable diligence timeframe for each state. States with historically long foreclosure timelines (New York — average 1,000+ days, New Jersey — 800+ days, Florida — 600+ days) have extended reasonable diligence windows. Missing these deadlines without documented cause results in interest curtailment on the FHA insurance claim.

Section 4 — CTL Impact of Timeline Compliance:
During CTL determination for FHA properties, verify the following timeline markers: (a) Date of default, (b) Date of first legal action, (c) Date of foreclosure sale, (d) Elapsed days from default to first legal action, and (e) Elapsed days from first legal action to foreclosure sale. If any timeline milestone exceeds HUD's reasonable diligence timeframe without a documented extension or delay reason, flag this in the CTL findings. Timeline non-compliance does not block CTL (the property can still be listed) but must be documented because it affects the insurance claim recovery.

Section 5 — Post-Foreclosure Conveyance vs. CWCOT:
After foreclosure of an FHA-insured property, the servicer has two paths: (a) Conveyance to HUD — the servicer conveys the property to HUD, and HUD disposes of the property. The servicer files an insurance claim. Conveyance must occur within 30 days of the foreclosure sale (or expiration of any redemption period). (b) CWCOT — the servicer retains the property and sells it directly, filing a claim for the shortfall. CWCOT properties do not require conveyance to HUD, which can accelerate disposition timelines significantly. The CTL determination should identify which path applies, as CWCOT properties have additional requirements per the CWCOT Program Policy.

Section 6 — Condition Requirements for FHA Properties:
For properties being conveyed to HUD (non-CWCOT path), HUD has specific property condition requirements that must be met before conveyance. The property must be: (a) secured against unauthorized entry, (b) cleaned of personal property and debris, (c) winterized in applicable climates, and (d) inspected with a documented condition report. Failure to meet condition requirements can result in rejection of conveyance or demand for re-conveyance allowance. For CWCOT properties being listed directly, condition requirements are governed by the as-is sale terms but minimum safety and marketing standards still apply.

Section 7 — FHA Case Number Verification:
Every FHA-insured property has an FHA case number. During CTL, verify that: (a) the case number is active and in good standing with HUD, (b) no open compliance findings, supplemental claims, or disputes exist on the case, and (c) the foreclosure type election (conveyance vs. CWCOT) has been properly recorded. An FHA case number in dispute or with open compliance findings requires resolution before CTL clearance.

References: Regulation X (12 CFR Part 1024, Subpart C — Mortgage Servicing). 24 CFR Part 203 (FHA Mortgage Insurance). HUD Handbook 4000.1 (FHA Single Family Housing Policy Handbook). HUD Mortgagee Letter 2016-16 (CWCOT Program).
